title: Shortlist - a store that turns your need into filters
pitch: An electronics store whose own filter vocabulary is the agent's tool schema - it ranks, explains what it hid, and can never un-veto a product you rejected.
about_excerpt: An electronics store whose own filter vocabulary is the agent's tool schema - it ranks, explains what it hid, and can never un-veto a product you rejected. Like Comment Story Updates The catalog: filters generated from real inventory Tool console: describe_catalog called live via WebMCP WebMCP surface: the tool's JSON Schema is generated live from the real catalog and filter vocabulary - the agent's tool surface and the store's own UI share one source of truth. Inspiration Every electronics store hides the answer behind its own vocabulary. A customer knows their need in plain language; the site offers RAM, sRGB percentage, and a price slider - the need turned into a quiz only the store understands. What it does Vidyut Electronics hands its own filter vocabulary to the agent as a tool. search_catalog 's JSON Schema is generated from the real catalog at boot - category, spec, and brand are enums of what the store actually sells - so the translation from need to constraints happens on the store page, visibly, not inside a black box. Every ranked result says what it satisfies and what it misses, with the actual value; near-misses say what would have to give; hidden listings say why. The human vetoes with one click, and no tool can ever bring a vetoed product back. How we built it One file, vanilla JavaScript, a fifteen-product seeded catalog with a deliberate trap (the strongest editor is a 2.3kg desk machine) and a deliberate near-miss. A single pure rank(query) function backs both the page's own render and every tool call, so the rail always shows exactly what the last tool call would return. Challenges we ran into Making the veto boundary airtight against a determined agent: add_to_shortlist has to refuse a vetoed id unconditionally and explain why, every time, including immediately after the agent re-searches and might plausibly try to re-add it thinking the veto was a UI-only state. Accomplishments that we're proud of A tool schema that's generated from real inventory data instead of hand-written - so the agent learns the store's actual vocabulary from the schema itself, and learns any gap in its guess from the error message, not from documentation. What we learned Wrapping every registerTool call in its own try/catch mattered in practice - one schema Chrome's validator disliked should cost one tool, never the whole surface. What's next The optional cross-origin stretch goal - exposing search_catalog to a separate origin via exposedTo / fromOrigins , so a comparison-shopping agent on another site could query Vidyut's catalog directly. Part of a seven-app portfolio Each entry proves a different WebMCP capability: Tablemap (dynamic tool registration), Signoff (a tool that only exists once a human approves it), Paperwork (structurally human-only fields), Jhola (genuinely cancellable long-running tools), Almari (quarantined untrusted content), Dhwani (declarative, no-JavaScript tools).
